claims.claim: On a drawloom, the warp threads to be lifted were selected by a second operator (the draw boy), not the weaver, making figured weaving slow and labour-intensive.
claims.episode_span: one weaver worked the treadles while a draw-boy or draw-girl pulled individual threads according to a memorized or paper diagram
claims.supporting_quote: The heddles with warp ends to be pulled up were manually selected by a second operator, the draw boy, not the weaver. The work was slow and labour-intensive, and the complexity of the pattern was limited by practical factors.

claims.claim: The Jacquard machine was controlled by a chain of punched cards, with one complete card corresponding to one row of the design.
claims.episode_span: He used rectangular cards pierced with holes; each hole allowed a needle to pass and lift its corresponding thread, while an unpunched spot kept the thread down.
claims.supporting_quote: Multiple rows of holes were punched on each card, with one complete card corresponding to one row of the design.

claims.claim: The punched-card loom mechanism was patented by Joseph Marie Jacquard in 1804.
claims.episode_span: Jacquard’s chain of punched cards moved the selection of threads outside any human head
claims.supporting_quote: The machine was patented by Joseph Marie Jacquard in 1804

claims.claim: The Jacquard machine's replaceable punched cards were an important conceptual precursor to computer programming and data entry, inspiring Babbage's Analytical Engine.
claims.episode_span: The same separation of instruction from execution later let early computing machines treat calculation steps as another kind of punched-card sequence.
claims.supporting_quote: The ability to change the pattern of the loom's weave by simply changing cards was an important conceptual precursor to the development of computer programming and data entry.

claims.claim: Joseph Marie Jacquard (1752-1834) demonstrated his loom in Lyon in 1801; it is controlled by a chain of punched cards that determine which warp cords rise for each pass of the shuttle.
claims.episode_span: A chain of such cards advanced automatically after every pick, so the loom itself read the pattern without further human interpretation.
claims.source_title: 1801: Punched cards control Jacquard loom | The Storage Engine | Computer History Museum
claims.supporting_quote: In Lyon, France, Joseph Marie Jacquard (1752-1834) demonstrated in 1801 a loom that enabled unskilled workers to weave complex patterns in silk. The Jacquard Loom is controlled by a chain of multiple cards punched with holes that determine which cords of the fabric warp should be raised for each pass of the shuttle.

claims.claim: The Lyon silk-weaver (canut) revolts of 1831 and 1834 turned on the piece prices merchants paid weavers: merchants cut prices in the late 1820s and the 1831 conflict centred on a minimum tariff for silk work, not on the machine.
claims.episode_span: the city's silk weavers later rose in the major Canut revolts of the 1830s, though those uprisings were driven chiefly by falling piece rates rather than by the machine itself
claims.supporting_quote: When a general strike was imminent on 25 October 1831, the prefect Louis Bouvier-Dumolart established a board of conciliation to supervise a minimum tariff for silk products.
